title: SeaCache: Efficient and Adaptive Caching for Sparse Accelerators
problem: Sparse tensor accelerators suffer from poor on-chip SRAM utilization because variable-length sparse fibers (rows/columns of nonzero data) do not map cleanly into fixed-size cache blocks, wasting capacity. Theoretically optimal replacement policies (e.g., Belady OPT) require expensive on-chip metadata that consumes significant die area.
motivation: Sparse workloads (GNNs, sparse transformers, recommendation models) are highly memory-bound, making effective on-chip data reuse critical to performance, yet existing cache designs leave substantial capacity unused due to fragmentation from variable-length sparse data.
method: SeaCache uses three techniques to make sparse caches more efficient. First, it reorganizes variable-length sparse data (rows or columns of nonzero values) by splitting long fibers across multiple cache blocks and grouping short fibers together, reducing wasted space. Second, instead of using an expensive way to decide which data to keep when the cache is full, it uses a practical approximation that exploits access patterns in sparse computations. Third, it dynamically adjusts how much cache space is reserved for data versus the metadata needed for these decisions, measuring the optimal split at runtime.
key_novelty: The core idea is a two-phase process that dynamically adjusts how the on-chip SRAM is split between sparse data and the metadata used to decide which data to keep, tuning their ratio at runtime to maximize space for variable-length fibers.
contributions: Fiber packing and splitting technique that achieves high space utilization when mapping variable-length sparse data into fixed-size cache blocks
A practical replacement policy that approximates optimal replacement with substantially lower implementation cost than prior metadata-heavy schemes
A two-phase adaptive mechanism that dynamically shares cache space between data and policy metadata, tuning partition ratios at runtime
End-to-end SeaCache design outperforming state-of-the-art sparse cache designs by 2.8x on average across sparse workloads
baselines: state-of-the-art sparse accelerator cache designs (on-demand caches with optimal replacement policies)
limitations: Evaluation scope and specific workload mix not fully described in abstract; metadata overhead of adaptive partitioning under adversarial access patterns is not discussed.
primary_theme: adaptive on-chip caching for sparse tensor accelerators
